questions.question_text: An investor deposits $\$800$ at the beginning of each year for $6\text{ years}$ into an account earning $6\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Which geometric series represents the future value $FV$?

options.why: Treated the annuity as ordinary with end-of-period payments, omitting the extra compounding factor.
Included only 5 terms instead of the required 6 terms for a 6-year annuity due.
Calculated compound interest on a single deposit rather than an annuity series.

questions.solution_text:
For start-of-year deposits, the first deposit compounds for $6$ years and the final deposit compounds for $1$ year.
$FV = 800(1.06) + 800(1.06)^{2} + \dots + 800(1.06)^{6}$

questions.question_text: A parent deposits $\$1500$ at the beginning of each year for $10\text{ years}$ into a savings fund earning $7\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Calculate the future value of the annuity.

options.why: Treated the annuity as ordinary with end-of-year payments, omitting the extra factor of $1.07$.
Calculated the sum of payments without applying any compound interest.
Added an extra payment term ($n = 11$) to the geometric series calculation.

questions.question_text: Maya invests $\$200$ at the beginning of each month for $5\text{ years}$ into an account earning $6\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. Find the balance after $5\text{ years}$.

options.why: Calculated future value for an ordinary annuity with end-of-month payments.
Multiplied payment by 60 months without calculating compound interest.
Used annual interest rate of $6\%$ instead of the monthly rate of $0.5\%$.

questions.question_text: A sports club deposits $\$900$ at the beginning of each quarter for $4\text{ years}$ into a reserve account earning $8\%$ p.a. compounded quarterly. Find the future value of the account.

options.why: Omitted the extra quarterly factor of $1.02$, treating it as an ordinary annuity.
Calculated simple principal total ($16 \times 900$) without interest.
Used $n = 4$ years instead of $n = 16$ quarterly compounding periods.

questions.question_text: A person wants to save $\$25\,000$ in $4\text{ years}$ with equal start-of-year deposits earning $6.5\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Calculate the required annual deposit $a$.

options.why: Calculated payment using ordinary annuity formula (end-of-year deposits).
Divided $\$25\,000$ by 4 years without accounting for interest.
Used $n = 5$ periods instead of $n = 4$ in the annuity-due formula.

questions.question_text: An investor deposits $\$1000$ each year for $15\text{ years}$ at $8\%$ p.a. compounded annually. By how much does the future value of an annuity due exceed that of an ordinary annuity?

options.why: Assumed the difference is simply one extra uncompounded payment.
Multiplied one annual deposit by the annual interest rate.
Calculated compound interest on one payment for 15 years.

questions.question_text: A saver deposits $\$400$ at the start of each month into an annuity earning $7.2\%$ p.a. compounded monthly. How much extra interest is earned over an $8\text{-year}$ term compared to making the deposits at the end of each month?

options.why: Assumed the difference is equal to exactly one monthly payment.
Calculated simple annual interest on a single monthly payment.
Multiplied monthly payment by 12 months.

questions.question_text: A company starts a $20\text{-year}$ endowment fund with annual contributions of $\$12\,000$ made at the beginning of each year earning $7.5\%$ p.a. compounded annually. Which expression gives the exact ratio of the future value of the first payment to that of the 20th payment?

options.why: Counted 20 compounding periods between the first and last start-of-year deposits.
Subtracted two periods instead of comparing deposit 1 ($20$ periods) to deposit 20 ($1$ period).
Multiplied the growth factor by the number of years instead of using powers.
